Home About

A small foundation, kept deliberately small.

Bridges of Light Foundation was founded in 2009 by four resettlement caseworkers who were tired of programs that ended at the airport. Seventeen years later, we are still the same shape — small enough to know every family, large enough to do real work in fourteen countries.

Mission

What we exist to do.

We help people cross borders with dignity, and we help ideas cross cultures with care. In practice, this means: legal casework, language tutoring, three-year resettlement follow-up, a standing emergency fund, and a literary-residency program that pairs writers across scripts and seas. We work in fourteen countries, with regional offices in Geneva, Amman, Tokyo, Beirut, and Berlin.

We are explicit about what we are not. We are not a frontline humanitarian agency — we hand off in emergencies to colleagues who do that work better. We are not a think tank. We do not publish policy briefs. We publish, instead, a quarterly letter about specific families and specific programs, with names changed where requested.

The foundation's name is a translation of a Persian phrase our founder, Layla Karim, heard from her grandmother in Tehran in the 1970s: پل‌های نور — "bridges of light." She said it meant the bridges built not from stone but from the small, repeated acts of welcome that hold people in place after a long journey.

At a glance

History

2009 to 2026, briefly.

The short version. The long version is in our annual reports.

2009

Founded in Geneva by Layla Karim, Tomáš Březina, Anaïs Roche, and Yuki Mori — four resettlement caseworkers, one shared post office box, one small grant from the Aga Khan Foundation.

2011

First regional office opens in Amman, supporting Iraqi refugee families. The Quarterly Letter publishes its first issue, mailed to 312 subscribers.

2013

Cultural Exchange program launches with a single Tokyo–Beirut translator residency. The first chapbook, Two Cities, One Sentence, is published in Arabic, Japanese, and French.

2015

Berlin office opens in response to Syrian arrivals across Europe. We commit to our three-year-follow-up model, which we still honour.

2018

Tokyo office opens. Education Bridges program launches with 24 students in its first cohort.

2020

Pandemic-year pivot: all casework moves to translated video calls. We do not lose a single family from our follow-up roster.

2022

Beirut office opens. Emergency Response fund formalised with CHF 2M reserve.

2024

Layla Karim steps down as Executive Director, becomes Chair Emerita. Amani Haddad succeeds her.

2026

3,200th family resettlement closed (i.e. completed three-year follow-up). The Quarterly Letter has 11,400 subscribers.

Leadership

The board.

Five trustees. They meet four times a year, in person, in rotating cities. They are unpaid.

Amani Haddad

Executive Director · Chair

Joined as a casework supervisor in 2014. Previously legal counsel at UNHCR Amman. Speaks Arabic, French, English. Based in Geneva.

Hiroshi Tanaka 田中 寛

Vice-Chair · Tokyo Region

Translator and editor. Founded the Tokyo office in 2018. Edits the Japanese edition of our Quarterly Letter. Based in Tokyo.

Layla Karim

Chair Emerita · Founder

Founding director, 2009–2024. Born in Tehran, raised in Geneva, trained as a refugee-law attorney. Continues to chair the Education Bridges advisory group.

Tomáš Březina

Treasurer · Co-Founder

Co-founder. Former municipal finance director, Prague. Audits our books before the auditors do. Based in Geneva.

Fatima Diallo

Trustee · Emergency Response

Twenty years at Médecins Sans Frontières, fifteen as field coordinator. Joined the board in 2020. Based in Dakar and Berlin.

Where we work

Four regions, one foundation.

Each region has a director with autonomy over local casework and a seat at headquarters.

Levant & Gulf

Amman · Beirut

Our largest casework footprint. Active in Jordan, Lebanon, Iraq, Egypt, and the United Arab Emirates. 1,420 active family files in 2025.

Director: Nour Al-Khoury · Amman

East Asia

Tokyo

Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan. Smaller in caseload, larger in cultural-exchange activity. Hosts the bilingual Tokyo translation cohort each spring.

Director: 小林 美咲 Misaki Kobayashi · Tokyo

Northern Europe

Berlin

Germany, Netherlands, Sweden, Denmark, and Poland. Most arrivals are second-stop families relocating from Greek or Italian first ports. 870 active files.

Director: Aisha Mwangi · Berlin

Mediterranean & HQ

Geneva

Headquarters, Swiss legal operations, southern-Europe casework partnerships in Italy, France, and Spain. The Quarterly Letter is edited here.

Director: Marco Bellini · Geneva
